cells.tense: Right now you're standing back and still inside it, tending what's growing because you can finally see how all of it fits together.
cells.ask: Offer the next step as something that can be finished — let yourself reach the end of one thing and set it down, and notice the ease that comes when you do.
cells.core:
You can see how the pieces fit together and you're tending them from that clear place. Nothing's being forced. What you look after gets your care because you know what it's for, and the people around you can feel it's held — including the ones who never say so. From up here you can tell which things need your hands and which are fine on their own, and you let the fine ones be.

The part of your life where you stand back and see the whole shape of things stays yours as long as you keep tending from there. This kind of care doesn't run out, and it doesn't need you to clutch anything. What's left is to let the finished things be finished — the seeing holds better when some of it's allowed to complete.
cells.sheetLine: You see how it all fits, and you tend it from there.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, careful hands
cells.place: up where the whole shape of it can be seen at once

cells.tense: You're ahead of the thing you're tending, seeing how it could all turn out and trying to steer every branch of it there before any of it has grown.
cells.ask: Let one piece of what you're tending go where it's already heading — see it whole and let it be finished as it is, and feel how much lighter seeing becomes when you're not also holding the outcome.
cells.core:
From up here the whole shape is visible and you can see what this could become. That sight is real, and when it's steady it tells you what to leave alone as much as what to do. The trouble is you're steering toward a picture that hasn't arrived. Every branch gets corrected toward how it should look. The care has gone tight and the load you're carrying is mostly the future.

Tending works best when it's got room. When every piece has to be shaped for an outcome that's still being imagined, nothing gets to grow on its own and you get nothing back for the holding. The picture can wait for the thing to catch up to it.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering a harvest that hasn't grown yet.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, careful hands
cells.place: up where the whole shape of it can be seen at once

cells.tense: You once saw how the pieces fit and pulled back from the whole shape of it, and you're still standing in the place where you stopped.
cells.ask: Keep following one thing you still hope for — not the outcome, just the hope — and let what you've already grown in this show you it's worth continuing.
cells.core:
From up here you'd see what you've made and how it holds, and there's more of it than it looks like from in close. You know that view — it's part of how you work. You're in the pieces instead: one thing, then another, kept going from the inside, with the whole shape staying out of view.

What brings the view back isn't trying harder to look. It's hoping for one thing again — the light you've stopped expecting is still what pulls the sight open, and it's the same light that shows you what you've grown. Effort won't do it. Wanting something will.
cells.sheetLine: You pulled back from the whole shape, and you're still standing there.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady, careful hands

cells.tense: You're reading the whole shape of it every day — you just never count that as something you're doing.
cells.ask: Say once, out loud, that you're the one looking after this — name what you've put into it, and let someone hear you say it.
cells.core:
The picture is there, you're reading it, and the reading is steering everything downstream — what you keep, what you let go. You talk about it like it's just what the situation calls for, as if the shape were sharpening itself.

The clear seeing is the thing you've made; you've just kept your name off it. That isn't a failure, it's a debt you owe yourself. And here's what's on the other side: admitting the care openly lets you set things down when they're finished, because the work's been seen. Not the whole story at once — one thing you've been tending, said as yours.
cells.sheetLine: You're reading the pattern — you just don't count it as yours.
